# Performance analysis

::: {.learning-objectives}
**Learning objectives**

- Produce the main descriptive bibliometric indicators.
- Distinguish productivity from citation impact.
- Account for unequal citation windows.
:::

## Main summary

```{r}
#| label: performance-load

source(here::here("R", "00_setup.R"))
M <- load_demo_data() |>
  mutate(
    DI = na_if(tolower(trimws(DI)), ""),
    TI = str_squish(TI),
    AU = str_to_upper(str_squish(AU))
  )

M <- M[!duplicated(M$DI) | is.na(M$DI), , drop = FALSE]
title_year <- paste(tolower(trimws(M$TI)), M$PY)
M <- tibble::as_tibble(M[!duplicated(title_year), , drop = FALSE])

results <- bibliometrix::biblioAnalysis(M, sep = ";")
summary_results <- summary(results, k = 15, pause = FALSE)
```

`biblioAnalysis()` provides publication counts, authorship, source, country, and citation summaries. These describe the corpus but do not explain why a paper or actor is influential.

## Annual scientific production

```{r}
#| label: annual-production

annual_output <- M |>
  count(PY, name = "publications")

ggplot(annual_output, aes(PY, publications)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c7fb8") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = pretty_breaks()) +
  labs(
    x = "Publication year",
    y = "Number of publications",
    title = "Annual FCM research output"
  )
```

Do not combine an incomplete current year with complete historical years without marking it clearly.

## Clinical composition over time

```{r}
#| label: indication-over-time

M |>
  count(PY, INDICATION) |>
  group_by(PY) |>
  mutate(percent = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(PY, percent, fill = INDICATION)) +
  geom_area(position = "stack") +
  labs(
    x = "Publication year",
    y = "Percentage of annual publications",
    fill = "Indication",
    title = "Changing clinical composition of the corpus"
  )
```

Counts answer how much was published. Percentages answer how the composition of the corpus changed. Report both when the total annual output changes substantially.

## Citation-window adjustment

Older publications have had more time to accumulate citations.

```{r}
#| label: citation-normalisation

M_citations <- M |>
  mutate(
    citation_window = pmax(1, 2025 - PY + 1),
    citations_per_year = TC / citation_window
  ) |>
  group_by(PY) |>
  mutate(
    year_mean_tc = mean(TC, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_normalised_tc = if_else(
      year_mean_tc > 0,
      TC / year_mean_tc,
      NA_real_
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

M_citations |>
  arrange(desc(citations_per_year)) |>
  select(SR, PY, TC, citation_window, citations_per_year, mean_normalised_tc) |>
  head(10)
```

Report the citation snapshot date and database. Avoid describing raw citation counts as study quality or clinical importance.

## Indicators worth retaining

- Annual publication count.
- Document-type distribution.
- Most relevant sources.
- Country and institution output.
- Total and fractional publication counts.
- Local and global citation counts.
- Citations per year or field/year-normalised citations.
- Missing citation and affiliation metadata.

Indicators such as Lotka's law, Bradford's law, and raw h-index rankings may be supplementary. They should not displace analyses linked to the research objectives.

## Exercise

Identify the ten papers with the highest raw citations and the ten with the highest citations per year. Explain why the lists differ.
